chapters.title: Chapter 1 – Arjuna Viṣāda Yoga (The Yoga of Arjuna’s Despondency)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Arjuna's Grief
chapters.description: The first chapter sets the stage for the entire dialogue of the Gita. It introduces Arjuna’s inner crisis — a conflict not just of duty but of identity, compassion, and despair. By showing Arjuna’s weakness and confusion, the text underscores the universal human struggle between worldly obligations and spiritual clarity. This chapter demonstrates that the Gita begins not from certainty but from doubt, making it a guide for seekers facing moral dilemmas in life.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 – Sāṅkhya Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Knowledge
chapters.description: This chapter is the foundation of the Bhagavad Gita. It is where Krishna begins his formal teaching, responding to Arjuna’s paralysis. Almost every major idea of the Gita is introduced here in seed form: the immortality of the soul, the importance of performing duty without attachment, the meaning of yoga as equanimity, and the portrait of the realized sage. For this reason, Chapter 2 is often seen as both a summary of the entire Gita and the framework that guides the rest of the dialogue.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 – Karma Yoga (The Yoga of Action)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Action
chapters.description: This chapter lays the foundation for one of the Gita’s central teachings — the path of selfless action. Krishna explains that outward renunciation is not necessary; what truly matters is the inner renunciation of attachment. Through right understanding and disciplined work, every act can become a means of liberation. Karma Yoga unites action, knowledge, and devotion, showing that spiritual growth happens not in withdrawal from life but through wise participation in it.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 – Jñāna-Karma-Sannyāsa Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge and Renunciation of Action)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Renunciation of Action in Knowledge
chapters.description: This chapter unites the paths of knowledge and action. Krishna reveals how divine wisdom transforms ordinary work into a means of liberation. He declares that he incarnates whenever righteousness declines, affirming that the divine takes form to restore balance. The teaching widens the concept of sacrifice — showing that inner understanding, not ritual, sanctifies life. Knowledge burns away ignorance and turns all action into worship.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 – Karma-Sannyāsa Yoga (The Yoga of Renunciation)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Renunciation
chapters.description: This chapter reconciles two paths that often appear opposed: renunciation (*sannyāsa*) and action (*karma-yoga*). Krishna explains that both can lead to liberation when practiced with detachment, but selfless action is usually superior because it purifies while keeping one engaged in life. True renunciation lies not in abandoning work but in surrendering the sense of ownership. The enlightened one performs action outwardly while resting inwardly in stillness — living as a free being amid the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 – Dhyāna Yoga (The Yoga of Meditation)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Meditation
chapters.description: This chapter offers one of the most practical teachings of the Gita — the discipline of meditation. Krishna explains that the true yogi is one who balances effort and rest, solitude and engagement, mind and body. Meditation becomes the bridge between action and silence. Through steady practice and detachment, the seeker learns to master the restless mind, achieving union with the divine Self that shines in all beings.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 – Jñāna-Vijñāna Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom
chapters.description: In this chapter, Krishna reveals the comprehensive nature of divine knowledge. He explains that both the material and spiritual worlds arise from his being — that God is simultaneously the substance and intelligence of the universe. The distinction between *jñāna* (intellectual understanding) and *vijñāna* (realized wisdom) becomes clear: it is not enough to know of God — one must perceive him everywhere. This chapter bridges philosophy and devotion, showing that love and knowledge are two faces of the same truth.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 – Akṣara-Brahma Yoga (The Yoga of the Imperishable Absolute)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Imperishable Brahman
chapters.description: This chapter explores the mystery of life, death, and immortality. Krishna reveals that the final thought at the moment of death determines the soul’s next state and that constant remembrance of the divine ensures liberation. He unites philosophy with devotion, showing that the highest wisdom is not abstract contemplation but unbroken awareness of God through love. The teaching transforms death from an end into a passage toward the eternal.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 – Rāja-Vidya Rāja-Guhya Yoga (The Yoga of Sovereign Knowledge and the Supreme Secret)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret
chapters.description: This chapter is often called the “heart” of the Gita. Krishna reveals the supreme knowledge that unites devotion, wisdom, and action into a single vision. He emphasizes that God pervades everything yet remains untouched by creation. Through loving faith, even the most ordinary acts become sacred. The message is intimate and universal: divine realization is available to all, regardless of background or merit.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 – Vibhūti Yoga (The Yoga of Divine Glories)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Divine Glories
chapters.description: Krishna here reveals how the divine presence can be perceived throughout creation. Everything noble, powerful, or beautiful is a spark of his infinite splendor. This chapter teaches that contemplation of divine manifestations strengthens devotion and expands perception, allowing the mind to rest in constant remembrance of God’s glory.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 – Viśvarūpa-Darśana Yoga (The Yoga of the Cosmic Vision)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of the Cosmic Vision
chapters.description: This chapter is the dramatic climax of the Gita’s revelation. Krishna grants Arjuna divine sight to behold his universal form — the boundless vision in which creation and destruction coexist. It is both terrifying and sublime, revealing the totality of existence as one living body of God. The experience transforms Arjuna’s understanding of the divine from philosophical concept to overwhelming reality.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 – Bhakti Yoga (The Yoga of Devotion)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Devotion
chapters.description: This chapter presents devotion (*bhakti*) as the most direct and accessible path to liberation. Krishna explains that love for the personal God leads swiftly to union with the impersonal Absolute. He highlights that devotion does not require learning, austerity, or complex rituals — only faith, surrender, and purity of heart. Bhakti turns knowledge into warmth and service, transforming life itself into an act of love.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 – Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña Vibhāga Yoga (The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of the Field and Its Knower
chapters.description: This chapter turns the focus inward, distinguishing the body and mind (the *field*) from consciousness (the *knower*). It is a philosophical and meditative exposition on the nature of reality. Krishna reveals that ignorance of this distinction causes bondage, while knowledge of it leads to freedom. The teaching integrates metaphysics with ethics: true wisdom expresses itself through humility, purity, and nonviolence.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 – Guṇa-Traya Vibhāga Yoga (The Yoga of the Division of the Three Guṇas)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of the Division of the Three Guṇas
chapters.description: Here Krishna analyzes the forces that shape human behavior. The three *guṇas* — *sattva* (harmony), *rajas* (activity), and *tamas* (inertia) — bind the soul to material existence. Understanding their interplay allows one to rise above them and live in spiritual freedom. The chapter serves as a psychology of liberation, showing how awareness transcends conditioning.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 – Puruṣottama Yoga (The Yoga of the Supreme Person)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of the Supreme Being
chapters.description: This chapter presents a profound vision of the world, the soul, and the Supreme Reality. Krishna describes the inverted cosmic tree — a vivid symbol of worldly existence rooted in the eternal but sprawling downward into entanglement. He distinguishes between the perishable world, the imperishable soul, and the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), who transcends both. This teaching encapsulates the essence of the Gita: realization of the eternal Self through detachment and devotion to the divine source.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 – Daivāsura Sampad Vibhāga Yoga (The Yoga of Divine and Demonic Qualities)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Divine and Demonic Qualities
chapters.description: Krishna here contrasts the divine and demonic natures that coexist within human beings. The divine qualities lead to freedom, harmony, and wisdom, while the demonic lead to bondage, chaos, and suffering. This chapter serves as a moral compass, showing that spiritual growth begins with cultivating virtue and self-control. It teaches that character is the vessel of realization — the divine must first be lived before it can be known.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 – Śraddhā-Traya Vibhāga Yoga (The Yoga of the Threefold Faith)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of the Threefold Faith
chapters.description: This chapter explores how faith (*śraddhā*) shapes every aspect of human life. Krishna explains that people act according to their inner disposition, and this disposition is governed by the three *guṇas* — *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.  Faith determines diet, worship, charity, and discipline.  By refining faith through understanding and intention, one converts everyday life into a sacred offering.  The chapter teaches that sincerity is not enough — faith must be guided by wisdom to lead toward liberation rather than bondage.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 – Mokṣa-Sannyāsa Yoga (The Yoga of Liberation and Renunciation)
chapters.subtitle: Yoga of Liberation and Renunciation
chapters.description: This final chapter gathers and completes all the Gita’s teachings.  Arjuna asks Krishna to clarify the difference between renunciation (*sannyāsa*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*).  Krishna synthesizes every path — knowledge, action, devotion, and renunciation — showing that true freedom arises when action is performed without attachment and offered to God.  The chapter culminates in the Gita’s supreme message: total surrender to the Divine Will as the final step to liberation.
